title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport
whyNow: The 2-4 hour blocks I keep saying I want have not appeared in four months, and I already know the argument for wanting them.
questions: What actually makes a block deep rather than merely uninterrupted?
Does the scheduling advice survive when the interruptions are other people I owe a reply to?
What does he say about work that is genuinely collaborative rather than solitary?
Which rule is load-bearing, and which are ornaments on it?

outsideView.replication: Not an empirical programme. The attention-residue result it leans on is Leroy 2009, one study, small, and narrower than the book's use of it. The 10,000-hour framing it borrows from Ericsson is contested by Macnamara's 2014 meta-analysis, which put deliberate practice at ~12% of variance across domains.
outsideView.critics: Read as absolutist about email and open offices. Practitioners in on-call, support and client-facing roles report the scheduling advice fails outright. Several reviewers note the exemplars are overwhelmingly tenured academics and solo authors — people with structural control over their calendars that most readers do not have.
outsideView.agedBadly: The 2016 social-media chapter predates short-form video, which is what most people now actually lose the hours to. The open-plan critique also predates the distributed-work shift, which changed the interruption channel from the desk to the notification.

parts.title: The idea
parts.outcome: Say what deep work is, why it is valuable and why it is becoming rare.

parts.title: The rules
parts.outcome: Run a week that actually contains depth, and say which rule produced it.

chapters.title: Deep work is valuable
chapters.argues: The two abilities that make a knowledge worker valuable in this economy both require sustained concentration, so depth is an economic input rather than a preference.

chapters.title: Deep work is rare
chapters.argues: Organisations destroy depth not out of malice but because visible busyness is the only productivity signal knowledge work has left.

chapters.title: Deep work is meaningful
chapters.argues: Depth is worth defending on craft and attention grounds even where the economic argument does not hold.

chapters.title: Work deeply
chapters.argues: Willpower is a finite daily budget, so depth has to be produced by a ritual and a schedule rather than by deciding to concentrate.

chapters.title: Embrace boredom
chapters.argues: The capacity for concentration is trained by what you do in the gaps, so scheduling distraction rather than scheduling focus is the lever.

chapters.title: Drain the shallows
chapters.argues: Shallow work expands to fill whatever it is given, so the only reliable control is a hard budget on it rather than better handling of it.

antiChapters.title: Rule #3 — Quit Social Media
antiChapters.reason: Settled for me already: I do not have the accounts, so reading it would be forty minutes of agreeing with myself rather than forty minutes of changing anything.

exitCondition: Four consecutive weeks in which at least three 90-minute blocks each week appear in the calendar, were actually worked, and the trigger that produced each one is named in the ledger.
